12328-tent-life-in-siberia-a-new-account:
George Kennan published Tent Life in Siberia in a revised edition in 1910, forty years after its first appearance in 1870. Kennan, later known for Siberia and the Exile System, here recounts a young man expedition among the Koraks and other tribes of Kamchatka and northern Asia.

The narrative follows the attempt to build a telegraph line across Siberia, with dog sleds, tents, and winter camps. A mid-book scene has a major pace nervously while news arrives from Russia: Lincoln murder, the rebellion end, and French invasion talk. Kennan writes with curiosity about native peoples and with humor about hardship. The book is a classic of American travel writing, from an age when Siberia seemed both remote and full of promise.
18216-pathfinders-of-the-west-being-the-:
A. C. Laut wrote Pathfinders of the West in 1904, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Remington and others. Laut tells the thrilling story of the men who found the great Northwest: Radisson, La Vérendrye, Lewis, and Clark.

Part one follows Radisson, the first white man to explore the West and North, captured by the Iroquois as a boy, tortured, adopted, and at last escaped. Later parts trace La Vérendrye and the Lewis and Clark trail. Laut writes with a historian's zeal and a storyteller's pace. It is a rousing, old history of the western paths.
24953-the-flemmings-and-flash-harry-of-s:
Louis Becke's stories from 'The Strange Adventure of James Shervinton,' published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, open with Martin Flemming, a restless trader settled on Chain Island, called Anaa by its people, in the Paumotu Group. At the populous village of Tuuhora he gains the respect of the Anaa people through just and honest dealing, never descending to a lie for gain. His wife, an intelligent Hawaiian ten years his junior, mothers their three half-caste children, aged thirteen, ten, and six.

A Marist Brother gives the children lessons several times a week, for which Flemming pays the mission liberally. The companion tale follows 'Flash Harry' of Savait and a search for news of four poor fellows seized by a Peruvian barque ten years earlier. Goddeffroy's great plantation lies a couple of miles from the anchorage. Becke's Pacific feels lived-in, rough, and unsentimental.
31673-the-rose-of-paradise-being-a-detai:
Howard Pyle's adventure novel, published by Harper and Brothers in 1888, is presented as the first published account of Captain John Mackra, written by Mackra himself. Its action is set in 1720, off the Island of Juanna in the Mozambique Channel, and involves the famous pirate Edward England.

Mackra's story moves from a pistol shot at an approaching boat to tense meetings, insults, and captures at sea, told in the voice of a seaman recalling danger firsthand. Readers get a swashbuckling pirate tale with illustrations, grounded in the routines and risks of early eighteenth-century sailing.

pathfinders-of-the-west-being-the-thrill:
Agnes C. Laut's Pathfinders of the West, copyrighted in 1904, tells the adventures of the men who opened the Great Northwest. The title names three of them: Radisson, La Vérendrye, and Lewis and Clark. Illustrations by Frederic Remington and others accompany the text.

In a letter at the front, Laut explains that while living in the Far West she tried to trace the explorers' paths herself. All the authorities led back to one main source of information. Her book turns that research into a lively narrative of fur traders, voyageurs, and the first crossings of a continent.
tent-life-in-siberia-a-new-account-of-an:
George Kennan wrote Tent Life in Siberia, an account of trips among the Koraks and other tribes in Kamchatka and northern Asia, with thirty-two plates and maps. Kennan also wrote Siberia and the Exile System and Campaigning in Cuba.

In a new preface dated by its own count to 1910, Kennan notes the tale first came out in 1870 and never went out of print. Its plates are near worn out from use, so he now adds more than fifteen thousand words he once cut for haste. Readers get sledges, tents, and tribal life at the far edge of Asia, from a man who crossed that cold land as a young telegraph scout.
